claim: In Escherichia coli, mutations at the mgrB locus were beneficial under trimethoprim exposure and led to overexpression of dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR), encoded by the folA gene.
source_text: We had previously (Patel and Matange, eLife , 2021) shown that, in Escherichia coli , mutations at the mgrB locus were beneficial under trimethoprim exposure and led to overexpression of dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR), encoded by the folA gene.
evidence_reasoning: This claim is supported by a reference to prior published work (Patel and Matange, eLife, 2021).

claim: DHFR levels are enhanced by spontaneous duplication of a genomic segment encompassing folA and spanning hundreds of kilobases.
source_text: Here, we show that DHFR levels are further enhanced by spontaneous duplication of a genomic segment encompassing folA and spanning hundreds of kilobases.
evidence_reasoning: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including immunoblotting and genome sequencing results.

claim: folA duplication was rare in wild-type E. coli.
source_text: This duplication was rare in wild-type E. coli .
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental observations comparing frequencies of duplications in wild-type versus lon-knockout strains.

claim: The frequency of folA duplication was elevated in a lon-knockout strain.
source_text: However, its frequency was elevated in a lon -knockout strain, altering the mutational landscape early during trimethoprim adaptation.
evidence_reasoning: This claim is supported by genome sequencing data showing higher frequency of GDA mutations in lon-knockout strains.

claim: During long-term evolution, folA duplications were frequently reversed.
source_text: During long-term evolution, folA duplications were frequently reversed.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by genome sequencing data from long-term evolution experiments showing loss of duplications over time.

claim: Reversal of folA duplication was slower under antibiotic pressure.
source_text: Reversal was slower under antibiotic pressure, first requiring the acquisition of point mutations in DHFR or its promoter.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by genome sequencing data showing temporal dynamics of duplication loss and point mutation acquisition under different selection pressures.

claim: Despite resistance-conferring point mutations, some populations under high trimethoprim pressure maintained folA duplication to compensate for low abundance DHFR mutants.
source_text: Unexpectedly, despite resistance-conferring point mutations, some populations under high trimethoprim pressure maintained folA duplication to compensate for low abundance DHFR mutants.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by genome sequencing and protein expression data from evolution experiments at high drug pressure.

claim: Evolution of gene dosage depends on expression demand, which is generated by antibiotic and exacerbated by proteolysis of drug-resistant mutants of DHFR.
source_text: We find that evolution of gene dosage depends on expression demand, which is generated by antibiotic and exacerbated by proteolysis of drug-resistant mutants of DHFR.
evidence_reasoning: This claim integrates multiple experimental observations including IC50 measurements, protein expression levels, and stability assays to infer the relationship between proteolysis and gene dosage.

claim: Proteostasis is a determinant of copy number evolution in antibiotic-resistant bacteria.
source_text: We propose a novel role for proteostasis as a determinant of copy number evolution in antibiotic-resistant bacteria.
evidence_reasoning: This is a synthesis claim based on experimental data showing the effects of Lon protease on both GDA frequency and DHFR mutant stability.

claim: Gene duplications and amplifications (GDAs) are implicated in cancer progression, speciation, reproductive isolation, and antimicrobial resistance.
source_text: Mutations that increase copy numbers, termed as gene duplications and amplifications (GDAs), are implicated in diverse biological phenomena including cancer progression (Dürrbaum and Storchová, 2016; Jiang et al., 2013; Spielmann et al., 2018), speciation (Pascual-Anaya et al., 2013; Taylor et al., 2001; Ting et al., 2004), reproductive isolation (Jiao et al., 2021; Maclean and Greig, 2011; Zuellig and Sweigart, 2018), and antimicrobial resistance (Elliott et al., 2013; Sandegren and Andersson, 2009).
evidence_reasoning: This claim is supported by multiple literature citations.

claim: GDAs are important for rapid adaptation since their frequencies of occurrence can be higher by several orders of magnitude than point mutations.
source_text: GDAs are important for rapid adaptation since their frequencies of occurrence can be higher by several orders of magnitude than point mutations (Elliott et al., 2013; Sandegren and Andersson, 2009; Anderson and Roth, 1981; Seaton et al., 2012; Sonti and Roth, 1989).
evidence_reasoning: This claim is supported by multiple literature citations.

claim: Amplified genes could be lost over time, pseudogenised, sub-functionalised, or neo-functionalised following the initial GDA mutation.
source_text: Following the initial GDA mutation, however, amplified genes could be lost over time, pseudogenised, sub-functionalised, or neo-functionalised (Hahn, 2009; Innan and Kondrashov, 2010; Kuzmin et al., 2022).
evidence_reasoning: This claim is supported by literature citations.

claim: In bacteria, GDA mutations are frequently encountered during adaptation to antibiotics or heavy metals.
source_text: In bacteria, GDA mutations are frequently encountered during adaptation to antibiotics (Sandegren and Andersson, 2009) or heavy metals (Hufnagel et al., 2021; von Rozycki and Nies, 2009).
evidence_reasoning: This claim is supported by literature citations.

claim: GDA mutations occur by RecA-dependent nonequal recombination as well as RecA-independent processes and often involve repeat sequences such as in IS-elements.
source_text: They occur by RecA-dependent nonequal recombination as well as RecA-independent processes and often involve repeat sequences such as in IS-elements (Bi and Liu, 1994; Reams et al., 2012; Reams et al., 2010; Reams and Neidle, 2003).
evidence_reasoning: This claim is supported by literature citations.

claim: As many as 20% of cells in a bacterial population may harbour a duplication of some genomic region.
source_text: Further, it is estimated that as many as 20% of cells in a bacterial population may harbour a duplication of some genomic region (Sun et al., 2012).
evidence_reasoning: This claim is supported by a literature citation.

claim: Dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) catalyses the NADPH-dependent reduction of tetrahydrofolate, an important cofactor in nucleotide and amino acid biosynthesis.
source_text: It catalyses the NADPH-dependent reduction of tetrahydrofolate, an important cofactor in nucleotide and amino acid biosynthesis.
evidence_reasoning: This is established biochemical knowledge about DHFR function.

claim: DHFR is coded by an essential gene in most organisms and its deletion or pharmacological inhibition results in cell death or growth stasis.
source_text: DHFR is coded by an essential gene in most organisms and its deletion or pharmacological inhibition results in cell death or growth stasis (Ahmad et al., 1998).
evidence_reasoning: This claim is supported by a citation and represents established knowledge about DHFR essentiality.

claim: Copy number amplification and consequent overexpression of DHFR confers resistance in cancer, malaria, and bacterial systems.
source_text: Interestingly, copy number amplification and consequent overexpression of DHFR confers resistance in all three systems (Brochet et al., 2008; Göker et al., 1995; Inselburg et al., 1987; Morales et al., 2009).

claim: In Escherichia coli DHFR is coded by folA.
source_text: In Escherichia coli DHFR is coded by folA.

claim: Several point mutations that confer trimethoprim resistance have been identified in DHFR.

claim: Mechanisms that transcriptionally upregulate folA expression include cis-regulatory mutations in the folA promoter and trans-acting loss-of-function mutations in mgrB.
source_text: Additionally, mechanisms that transcriptionally upregulate folA expression are also known in trimethoprim-resistant E. coli. These include cis-regulatory mutations in the folA promoter and trans-acting loss-of-function mutations in mgrB, which upregulate folA transcription in a PhoQP-dependent manner (Baym et al., 2016; Palmer et al., 2015; Patel and Matange, 2021; Toprak et al., 2011).
